groups.etymology: Inherited from Old French nagier, inherited from a reduced form of Latin navigāre. Doublet of naviguer, a later borrowing. Displaced Old French noer, from Latin natāre, natō (“to swim”).

ex.fr: Il est vraiment naïf, il a gobé tout ce qu'ils lui ont raconté.
ex.en: He is really naive; he swallowed everything that they told him.

groups.etymology: Inherited from Old French naïf, inherited from Latin nātīvus. Doublet of natif. Semantical shift from "original; natural; simple" to "simple-minded".
From Old French naissance (12th c.), derived after Latin nāscentia (“birth”). By surface analysis, naître + -ance. Compare Catalan naixença, Occitan naissença.
Inherited from Middle French naistre, from Old French naistre, from Latin nascere.
Diminutive form of Anna, Anne, popularised after Émile Zola's 1880 novel Nana.

senses.d: layer (of gas, oil etc.); sheet (of water)

groups.etymology: From Latin mappa.

senses.d: inflection of napper (first/third-person singular present indicative/subjunctive)

groups.etymology: Inherited from Middle French nation, from Old French nacion, borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tisder. Proto-Italic *gnātiō Latin nātiōlbor.

ex.fr: C'est que, rompant avec l'imitation des siècles précédents, ils retournent à l'éternelle inspiratrice, à la nature . . .
ex.en: For, breaking with the imitation of previous centuries, they return to the eternal inspirer—to nature . . .

groups.etymology: Inherited from Middle French nature, Old French nature, borrowed from Latin nātūra.

groups.etymology: Inherited from Middle French naturel, from Old French natural, a borrowing from Latin nātūrālis. By surface analysis, nature + -el.

phrases: zone naturelle d'intérêt écologique, faunistique et floristique

groups.etymology: From naturel + -ment.

Inherited from Middle French navire, from Old French navirie, variant of navilie, probably from Vulgar Latin *navilium (compare Old Occitan navili), alteration of Classical Latin navigium (whence also Old French navoi, navie).
Probably from Latin ne gentem ("no person, no one"), or ne entem (“not existing”). Compare Italian niente.

ex.fr: Il est nécessaire qu'on fasse l'amour.
ex.en: It is necessary that we make love.

groups.etymology: From Old French necessité (12th c.), a borrowing form Latin necessitās.

groups.etymology: From Middle French nege, naige (14th c.), deverbal from neiger (“to snow”). Displaced related Old French noif, from Latin nix, nivem.

ex.en: Put some muscle into it, boys! We are not on a pleasure boat!

groups.etymology: Inherited from Middle French nerf, from Old French nerf, inherited from Latin nervus.
Inherited from Middle French nerfveux, from Old French nerveus, a borrowing from Latin nervōsus.
From Old French net, inherited from Latin nitidus (“shiny”) through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nittus. Doublet of nitide, a borrowing.

Inherited from Middle French nettoyer, from Old French netoiier, a restructuring (based on net (“clean (adj.)”)) of Old French noiier (“to clean”), from Vulgar Latin *nitidiāre, a verb based on Latin nitidus (“shining, polished”), which took on the meaning of 'clean'.

Inherited from Middle French nez, from Old French nés, from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Compare Italian naso.

From nombre + -eux, or from Latin numerōsus.

phrases: se noyer dans un verre d'eau

groups.etymology: Inherited from Middle French nu, from Old French nu, from Latin nūdus, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós.
